ops.title: flock on darwin excludes two OFDs in one process — the in-process gate guarded nothing
ops.body:
Measured 2026-08-01 by the P4.1 Lane A refuter, running the primitive rather than reasoning about
it. Two `os.OpenFile` handles on one path, one process:

    same-process two-fd flock: first=<nil> second=resource temporarily unavailable

So `flock(2)` on darwin excludes two independent open file descriptions within a single process. The
phase-4 design asserted the opposite in `durable.Lock`'s godoc — "two goroutines opening the same
lock file hold independent open-file descriptions and can both flock it" — and justified ~46 lines
of process-global mutable map (a `map[cleanPath]*gate` of one-slot channels, refcounted) on it.

The confusion is `flock()` versus `fcntl()` record locks. `fcntl` locks are per-process and WOULD
silently let two goroutines both "hold" one; `flock` locks are per-OFD and exclude. daemonkit uses
flock, so the guard was never load-bearing.

Proven functionally as well as by measurement: deleting `gateFor`/`enter`/`leave`/`retire` and both
call sites left `TestAcquireLockExcludesGoroutines` (8 goroutines, peak holders must be 1) passing
under `-race` — i.e. the test naming the property could not fail either way.

Consequence taken: the gate is deleted per STYLEGUIDE §1 ("no guards against impossible states") and
the godoc corrected, in `durable/lock.go` and in the design of record. A public godoc stating a
falsehood is worse than the dead code, because a consumer reasons from it.

Secondary detail found on the way: the gate keyed on `filepath.Clean(path)` rather than a canonical
path, so `/tmp/x.lock` and `/private/tmp/x.lock` got different gates — harmless only because flock
already excluded.
